title: Business Organisation and Management

pattern.summary: 9 questions, attempt any 5, each carries 20 marks. All theory. The last 2–3 questions are usually short notes, 'distinguish between' or 'comment on' with internal choice.

sessionNotes.2023-06: The printed sub-marks add to 10 per question, but the paper is 100 marks with 5 equal questions, so each is counted as 20.

choosing: The paper is entirely theory. Planning, organisation structure, leadership, motivation and marketing (PLC, pricing) return almost every session.
Questions with internal choice ('any two of the following') are good picks — you choose the notes you know.

topics.name: Planning
topics.summary: Meaning, nature, importance, principles, process; plans vs policies; long vs short range.
points: Planning: setting future objectives and deciding in advance how to achieve them. It comes before all other management functions (primacy) and runs through every level (pervasive).
Nature: future-oriented yet based on past and present information, purposeful, intellectual yet action-oriented, involves decision-making, rests on assumptions and is continuous and dynamic.

Importance: gives direction, lets managers compare alternatives, cuts impulsive and ad hoc decisions, is the base of other functions, allocates scarce resources, helps adapt to change and spot threats and opportunities early.
Limitations: forecasts may be wrong, information may be unreliable or late, the environment changes beyond control, planning delays action and can make managers rigid.

Process (book): planning to plan → appraise internal conditions → appraise external environment → define key areas and issues → develop and choose alternative plans → form medium- and short-range plans → arrange implementation.

Types: by comprehensiveness — strategic (organisation-wide moves against competition) vs tactical (specific functional sub-plans); by time — long-range vs short-range (one year or less, more detailed).
Plans are single-use (for unique, non-repetitive situations, e.g. programmes, budgets) or standing (for repeated situations, e.g. policies, procedures, rules, methods).
Plan vs policy: a plan is a course of action to reach a goal; a policy is a standing plan — a general guide to thinking and decisions (e.g. 'promote from within').
Principles: top management interest, long-range view, contribution to objectives, primacy, flexibility, navigational change, commitment and the limiting factor.
topics.frame: Definition (quote Koontz: 'deciding in advance what to do, how to do it, when to do it and who is to do it') → headed points → a flow diagram of the process → conclusion.
mistakes: Listing process steps without one line of explanation each.
examples:
Example: a bakery plans for Diwali
Objective: sell 2,000 sweet boxes in the festival week. Looking at last year's sales and this year's orders, the owner compares alternatives (hire temporary staff or run a second shift), chooses the second shift, and makes a short-range plan: buy ingredients by a set date, fix the shift roster, book delivery vans.
Standing plan: a policy of 'no credit sales above ₹5,000'. Single-use plan: the budget for this one festival week.

topics.name: Organisation Structure
topics.summary: Types of structure (line, functional, line & staff), formal vs informal, departmentation, span of control, charts and manuals.
points: Organising: identifying and grouping activities and fixing authority–responsibility relationships so people can work together towards goals; its result is the organisation.
An organisation is a system: inputs (people, materials, information) → processor (throughput) → outputs (goods and services).
Steps: set objectives → identify and group activities → allot duties → establish relationships.
Structures by arrangement of activities: functional, divisional and adaptive (project and matrix organisation).
Principles include unity of objectives, specialisation, chain of command, unity of command, span of supervision, exception, balance, flexibility and continuity.
Span of control: how many people a manager can supervise well; depends on the nature of work, abilities of the manager and subordinates, and staff help.
Organisation chart: diagram of positions and lines of authority. Organisation manual: written record of policies, procedures and job descriptions.
Formal organisation is the officially planned structure; informal organisation grows from people's social and psychological needs.
Departmentation: grouping activities by function, product, territory, customer, process or project; it brings specialisation, control, clear responsibility and manager development.

Forms of authority: line (scalar/military — direct chain from top to bottom), line and staff (line commands, staff advise; the two may clash) and functional (the book advises limiting it to the top levels).
topics.frame: Meaning → draw a small chart of the structure → features → merits and demerits in two lists → suitability.
mistakes: Not drawing a chart — a simple diagram earns marks.

units.title: Departmentation and Forms of Authority Relationships

examples:
Example: a growing garment firm organises itself
Activities are grouped into departments — purchase, production, sales, accounts (functional departmentation). Each department head reports to the general manager (chain of command) and each worker reports to one supervisor (unity of command).
When the firm starts selling in three states it adds regional sales managers for North, South and West — territorial departmentation within the sales department.
A line-and-staff touch: a legal adviser advises the general manager but gives no orders to the workers.

topics.name: Marketing (Concepts, PLC, Pricing)
topics.summary: Marketing concepts, marketing mix, product life cycle and pricing — asked in almost every paper.
points: Marketing (Kotler): 'human activity directed at satisfying needs and wants through exchange processes' — finding consumer needs, turning them into products and moving them to consumers profitably.
Five marketing concepts: production, product, selling, marketing and societal.
Selling converts the product into cash; marketing is the whole process of identifying, meeting and satisfying consumer needs.
Marketing matters to the business, consumers, the economy and society; in a developing economy its benefits are not fully realised.
Marketing mix (the book's four Ps): product, price, promotion and physical distribution (place).
Product life cycle: introduction → growth → maturity → decline (obsolescence); knowing the stage helps plan strategy.
Prices depend on cost, demand and competition, giving cost-oriented, demand-oriented and competition-oriented pricing.
topics.frame: Definition → a PLC curve diagram (sales vs time) → each stage with features and strategy → conclusion.
examples:
Example: a new ready-to-cook millet mix through its life cycle
Introduction: few buyers, heavy promotion and free samples, low or no profit.
Growth: sales rise fast, competitors enter, more shops stock it.
Maturity: sales level off; the firm offers new flavours and price packs to defend its share.
Decline: tastes change and sales fall; the firm cuts costs or withdraws the product.

Example: selling concept vs marketing concept
Selling concept: a firm has unsold stock of heavy steel cupboards and pushes them through discounts and aggressive salesmen.
Marketing concept: the firm first finds that young renters want light, foldable cupboards, designs one, prices it for them and sells it online — satisfying the need at a profit.

topics.name: Leadership & Morale
topics.summary: Meaning, styles, qualities of a leader, manager as leader, and morale.
points: Leadership: influencing, guiding and directing people to secure their willing cooperation towards goals. A manager who also leads gets both task results and human satisfaction.

Theories: trait (success depends on personality traits), behavioural (leaders known by how they behave with followers) and situational (depends on leader–follower relations, task structure and position power).
Styles: autocratic (power centralised — low morale over time), democratic (decisions with group participation — better morale and growth) and laissez-faire (group left to decide — risk of chaos).
Functions: build teamwork, represent the group and link it to top management, advise and counsel, manage work schedules, use power properly.

Managerial grid: styles judged by concern for people and concern for work. More effective: executive, developer, benevolent autocrat, bureaucrat. Less effective: compromiser, missionary, autocrat, deserter.
Qualities of an effective leader: physical and mental health, empathy, self-confidence, self-awareness, objectivity, knowledge, decisiveness, ability to communicate.
topics.frame: Definition → styles with one example each (table: style / features / suitable when) → conclusion.
examples:
Example: three styles, one decision
A factory must change its shift timings.
Autocratic: the manager announces the new timings and expects compliance — quick, but workers resent it.
Democratic: the manager discusses options with worker representatives and they agree on a timing — slower, but morale and acceptance are higher.
Laissez-faire: the manager tells workers to sort it out themselves — confusion if the group cannot agree.

topics.name: Motivation & Incentives
topics.summary: Meaning, process, Maslow and Herzberg theories, financial vs non-financial incentives.
points: Motivation: the forces that make a person willing to use their full ability to achieve objectives. Motives (needs) start the process.
Nature of motives: invisible, one motive can cause many behaviours and one behaviour many motives, they can conflict and change over time.
Elements of the process: behaviour, motives, goals and feedback.
McGregor: Theory X assumes people dislike work and must be pushed; Theory Y assumes people like work and can direct and control themselves.
Maslow: needs arise in order — physiological → security → social → esteem → self-fulfilment.

Herzberg: hygiene (maintenance) factors like pay, security and working conditions only prevent dissatisfaction; motivators like recognition and achievement motivate. Job enrichment (vertical loading — more responsibility and challenge) differs from job enlargement (horizontal loading — more tasks of the same kind).

Types: positive (rewards) vs negative (fear, demotion, lay-off); extrinsic (off the job, financial) vs intrinsic (on the job, self-actualisation); financial (wages, bonus, benefits) vs non-financial (praise, competition, participation, growth).
topics.frame: Definition → theory with a pyramid diagram (Maslow) or two-column table (Herzberg) → criticism → conclusion.
mistakes: Drawing Maslow's pyramid in the wrong order.
examples:
Example: Maslow and Herzberg at a call centre
Pay on time and a safe office meet physiological and security needs — they are hygiene factors: without them staff are dissatisfied, but more of them does not motivate much.
A 'best agent of the month' award (esteem) and a chance to lead a small team (self-fulfilment, job enrichment) are motivators.
Job enlargement would be simply giving an agent more calls of the same kind; job enrichment gives them the authority to settle complaints themselves.

topics.name: Innovation, Skill Development & Start-ups
topics.summary: Innovation types and process, skill development initiatives, Start-up India, Make in India, MSMEs.
points: Creativity is having new, useful ideas; invention is a new product or process idea; innovation turns an idea or invention into a good or service customers will pay for.
Types of innovation in the book: incremental, disruptive, architectural and radical.

Make in India: government drive to get firms (including through FDI) to set up manufacturing in India, for jobs and GDP growth. 'Made in India' is the tag on goods made with Indian land, labour, capital, enterprise and technology.
Digital India (2015): aims to make India a digital nation, speed up work and link rural and urban areas.

Skill development is led by the Ministry of Skill Development and Entrepreneurship (MSDE): Indian Institute of Skills, Pradhan Mantri Kaushal Vikas Yojana, National Apprenticeship Promotion Scheme, dual system of training, space-based distance learning.

Startup India (2016) builds a friendly ecosystem for start-ups. Its action plan has three pillars: simplification and handholding; funding support and incentives; industry-academia partnership and incubation.
An incubator is an organisation that helps start-ups grow faster and succeed (space, guidance, access to funds).
topics.frame: Meaning → steps in a flow chart → Indian examples (schemes, companies) → conclusion.
examples:
Example: from idea to start-up
Creativity: a student notices farmers selling vegetables cheaply because they spoil. Invention: a low-cost solar cold box. Innovation: turning it into a product farmers rent per day, so they can sell later at a better price.
The founder registers under Startup India, joins a college incubator for space and mentoring, and trains local technicians through a skill-development scheme.

topics.name: CSR & Business Ethics
topics.summary: Corporate social responsibility, its paradigm shift and theories, and components of business ethics.
points: Social responsibility of business (CSR) is the role business plays in society — acting for the good of society, not only for profit.

The book's three CSR theories: CSR theory (voluntary contributions to community welfare), stakeholder theory (stakeholders' interests must shape decisions) and the triple bottom line (profit, people, planet).
Business ethics is applied ethics — moral principles in business decisions. It is wrong to treat ethics as only a personal trait and CSR as only charity; both come from moral philosophy.
Corporate responsibility = CSR + corporate governance + environmental accountability.

Paradigm shift: NGOs, media reach, scandals (Enron, Satyam), socially responsible investors and aware consumers pushed business to go beyond philanthropy. First shift — business is a social institution, not just property; second shift — responsibility towards society.

India's framework: the CSR Voluntary Guidelines (2009) with six components — care for all stakeholders, ethical working, workers' rights and welfare, human rights, environment, social and inclusive development; then the National Voluntary Guidelines (2011).

Mandatory rule: Section 135 and Schedule VII of the Companies Act, 2013 (from 1 April 2014) — a company with net worth ₹500 crore, turnover ₹1,000 crore or net profit ₹5 crore must spend at least 2% of its average net profit of the last three years on CSR.
Not counted as CSR: activities in the normal course of business, contributions to political parties, and activities outside India.
topics.frame: Definition → points with headings → Indian example (e.g. Tata, Infosys) → conclusion.
examples:
Example: does the CSR rule apply, and how much?
A company's net profit for the last three years is ₹9 crore, ₹12 crore and ₹15 crore. Net profit above ₹5 crore brings it under Section 135.
Average net profit = (9 + 12 + 15) ÷ 3 = ₹12 crore; minimum CSR spend = 2% × 12 = ₹0.24 crore (₹24 lakh).
Funding a village school's library counts; a donation to a political party, or spending on its own employees' routine welfare as part of normal business, does not.

topics.name: E-commerce & Emerging Trends
topics.summary: E-commerce vs traditional commerce, m-commerce, Digital India, outsourcing, franchising.
points: The internet has changed how firms operate and talk to customers. Internet of Things: a network of devices that connect and exchange data.
Emerging trends listed in the book: automation, blockchain, artificial intelligence, machine learning, social shopping, robotics, e-tailing and retail entrepreneurship.
Technology brings both opportunities and threats; benefits include lower costs, smoother communication and room to expand.

E-commerce: doing business, including customer service, over the internet; it gives access to large markets. Features include real-time shopping, mobile apps, multi-channel selling, big data, personalisation, push notifications and social media.
M-commerce is e-commerce on mobile devices. An e-wallet is a virtual wallet you load with money to make digital payments.
Franchising: the franchisor (owner of the original business) sells the right to use its brand and system to a franchisee.
Outsourcing: contracting a third party to do certain functions to cut costs. Offshoring: moving a business process from one country to another.
topics.frame: Definition → comparison table (traditional vs e-commerce) → merits and limitations → conclusion.
examples:
Example: one small shop, many trends
A handloom shop sells on its own website and on an app (e-commerce, m-commerce), accepts payment through e-wallets and UPI, and sends push notifications about new arrivals.
It outsources delivery to a courier company and its bookkeeping to an accountant's firm. Later it lets a trader in another city open a shop under its name and design (franchising), in return for a fee.

topics.name: Business, Commerce, Trade & Profession
topics.summary: Business vs profession vs employment, commerce, trade and aids to trade, industry, objectives of business.
points: Human activities are economic (done to earn a living) or non-economic (done out of love, duty, religion or social feeling).

Economic activities are of three kinds: business (producing or exchanging goods and services for profit), profession (personal, specialised service needing training, e.g. doctor, lawyer) and employment (working for an employer under a contract or service rules).
Features of business: deals in goods or services, production and/or exchange, regular dealings, profit motive, risk and enterprise.
Objectives of business go beyond profit: economic, social and human objectives.
Business = industry + commerce. Industry: extractive (mining), genetic (breeding plants and animals), manufacturing and construction.
Commerce = trade (buying and selling) + aids to trade — transport, warehousing, banking, insurance and advertising — which remove hindrances and keep goods moving.
Four basic forms of business organisation: sole proprietorship, partnership, company and cooperative society.
An entrepreneur conceives the business idea, gathers the resources and brings the organisation into being; common traits are independence, hard work, drive to achieve, open mind and optimism.
MSMEs are grouped into manufacturing enterprises and service enterprises (services are measured by investment in equipment).
topics.frame: Definition → classification chart → table comparing business, profession and employment → conclusion.
examples:
Examples: classify the activity
A doctor running a clinic → profession. A nurse working in a hospital for a salary → employment. A shopkeeper selling groceries → business (trade). A farm growing flower seedlings to sell → genetic industry. A mother cooking for her family → non-economic activity.
Aids to trade in one sale: a Kerala spice trader's goods travel by truck (transport), wait in a warehouse (warehousing), are insured (insurance), paid for through a bank (banking) and promoted online (advertising).

topics.name: Joint Stock Company & Public Enterprises
topics.summary: Company features and types, private vs public, OPC, government companies, Maharatna/Navratna/Miniratna.
points: Company: an artificial person created by law, with a separate legal entity, common seal and perpetual succession; ownership (shareholders) is separate from management (directors).
Members: public company minimum 7, no maximum; private company minimum 2, maximum 200. The Companies Act, 2013 also allows a One Person Company and a Small Company.
Other features: limited liability, free transfer of shares (restricted in a private company), rigid objects (the object clause of the Memorandum) and heavy statutory regulation.

Classification — by incorporation: statutory, registered, chartered; by liability: unlimited, limited by guarantee, limited by shares; by ownership: private, public, government company; by jurisdiction: national, multinational.
Company — merits: limited liability, transferable shares, stability, easy to raise capital, expert management. Demerits: costly and hard to form, heavy regulation, little secrecy, slow decisions.
Public enterprise: a business owned and managed by central, state or local government whose output is sold, run for social welfare and accountable to the legislature.

Three forms of public enterprise: departmental undertaking (run like a government department, financed by the budget, staff are civil servants), public (statutory) corporation (created by a special Act, financially autonomous, staff are not civil servants) and government company.

Government company: at least 51% of paid-up capital held by the central and/or state governments; registered under the Companies Act. When private investors also hold shares it is a mixed-ownership company.

Ratna schemes give the boards of profit-making central public enterprises more powers: Maharatna (2010, for mega enterprises to become global giants — e.g. Coal India, BHEL, IOC, NTPC, ONGC, SAIL), Navratna (1997, e.g. BEL, HAL) and Miniratna (1997, Category-I and II). The lists change over time.
topics.frame: Definition → features as headed points → types in a chart → merits and limitations → conclusion.
examples:
Example: private or public company?
Five family members form 'Kumar Foods Private Limited' — allowed, since a private company needs at least 2 members (up to 200) and restricts transfer of shares.
To raise money from the public for a big factory it later becomes a public company: it needs at least 7 members and its shares can be freely transferred on a stock exchange.
If the government holds 51% or more of the paid-up capital of a company, it is a government company.

Example: limited liability
A shareholder holds 1,000 shares of ₹10, fully paid. If the company fails with large debts, the shareholder loses at most ₹10,000 — the amount invested; creditors cannot claim personal property.

topics.name: Decision-Making
topics.summary: Meaning, relationship with planning, and the steps of scientific decision-making.
points: A decision is a choice among alternatives about what should or should not be done (Drucker; McFarland).
Three elements: an act of choice, possible alternatives, and a conclusion (picking the best).
Process: identify the problem or opportunity → explore alternatives → evaluate them → select the best → implement → follow up.
A problem endangers the organisation's ability to reach its objectives; an opportunity offers a chance to exceed them.
Planning and decision-making go together: planning is itself a series of decisions about the future.
topics.frame: Definition → flow chart of steps → one example → conclusion.
examples:
Example: a shop's sales are falling
Problem: sales down 20% since a supermarket opened nearby.
Alternatives: cut prices, start home delivery, or stock specialty local products.
Evaluate: price cuts hurt margin; delivery needs a boy and a bike (low cost); specialty products need new suppliers.
Select: start home delivery through phone orders. Implement it, then follow up by checking sales after two months.

topics.name: Co-operative Organisation
topics.summary: Meaning, features, types, merits, limitations and objectives of co-operatives.
points: A cooperative is a voluntary association of people who are not financially strong on their own and come together for self-help and mutual help — not mainly for profit.
Features: voluntary and open membership, democratic control, service motive, separate entity on registration, limited liability, state help and control.
Merits: easy to form, limited liability, government assistance, open membership.
Demerits: lack of business skill, weak mutual interest, no secrecy, rivalry among members.
The book suits the cooperative form to cases where the interest of a particular section of society has to be looked after.
topics.frame: Definition → features → types → merits and limitations table → Indian example.
examples:
Example: a milk producers' cooperative
Small dairy farmers in a village each have two or three cows and are exploited by middlemen. They form a cooperative society, each buying a share. Every member has one vote whatever their shareholding (democratic control).
The society collects milk, tests it, sells it to a dairy and pays members fairly — service, not profit, is the aim. Anyone in the village who keeps cows may join (open membership).

topics.name: Sole Proprietorship & Partnership
topics.summary: Sole trader features, partnership deed, kinds of partners, sole vs partnership.
points: Sole trader: owned, financed and controlled by one person; no legal difference between owner and business; best for small business.

Sole trader — merits: full control, secrecy, easy and cheap to form and close, little regulation. Demerits: unlimited liability, limited capital and management skill, unstable life, hard to attract good staff.

Partnership (Indian Partnership Act, 1932): 'the relation between persons who have agreed to share the profits of a business carried on by all or any of them acting for all.' Minimum 2 partners; the book gives a maximum of 50 under the Companies Act, 2013.

Features: two or more persons, agreement (oral, written or implied), profit sharing, a lawful business, mutual agency (each partner is an agent of the firm and the others), unlimited liability, good faith, no transfer of share without everyone's consent.

Kinds of partners — by participation: active (working) and sleeping (dormant); by profit sharing: nominal (lends only the name) and partner in profits (shares profits, not losses — e.g. a minor); by conduct: partner by estoppel and by holding out; by liability: limited and general.
Partnership — merits: more capital and skills, more stable than a sole trader, incentive to key staff. Demerits: unlimited liability, hard to transfer shares, conflicts among partners, short life.

Partnership deed: the written agreement, stamped and registered. It covers the firm's name and business, partners' names, place of business, capital of each partner, profit-sharing ratio, loans, drawings and interest, interest on capital, duties and pay of partners, accounts and audit, goodwill and revaluation on admission, retirement or death, and settlement on dissolution.
topics.frame: Definition → features → merits and limitations → table comparing sole trader and partnership.
examples:
Example: sole trader to partnership
Ravi runs a mobile repair shop alone — full control and secrecy, but if the shop owes ₹2 lakh and its assets are only ₹50,000, Ravi's personal savings can be taken (unlimited liability).
To open a second shop he takes Meena as a partner who brings ₹3 lakh, and Arun as a sleeping partner who only invests. Their deed fixes capital, profit-sharing ratio, interest on capital and what happens if one retires. Each partner can bind the firm (mutual agency).

topics.name: Delegation of Authority
topics.summary: Meaning, principles, and why managers and subordinates avoid delegation.
points: Delegation: giving a subordinate formal authority and responsibility for certain work. Elements: entrusting duties (responsibility), granting authority and creating accountability.
Benefits: better use of resources, lighter load on top executives, better decisions, initiative and self-development of subordinates.
Why managers don't delegate: no confidence in subordinates, fear of losing power, lack of self-confidence.
Why subordinates avoid it: prefer to avoid responsibility, fear of criticism, lack of resources, lack of motivation.
Making it work: climate of trust, clear objectives, clearly defined authority and responsibility, motivation, good communication and training.
Centralisation keeps authority with top managers; decentralisation is systematic delegation to all levels of the organisation. Delegation leads to decentralisation.
Degree of decentralisation depends on size, rate of growth, nature of the organisation, management philosophy and environment; neither extreme is desirable — the book calls for a 'golden mean'.
topics.frame: Definition → the three elements → principles → barriers and how to overcome them.
examples:
Example: a principal delegates
The principal of a college entrusts the annual sports day to a senior teacher (responsibility), lets them spend up to ₹50,000 and pick volunteers (authority), and asks for a report afterwards (accountability).
The principal remains finally accountable to the management — authority can be delegated, ultimate responsibility cannot. When such delegation happens in every department systematically, the college becomes decentralised.

topics.name: Communication
topics.summary: Process, barriers and making communication effective.
points: Communication: exchange of facts, ideas, opinions or feelings between two or more persons. It is two-way and is complete only when the receiver understands and responds.
Elements: communicator, encoding, message, medium, decoding, receiver and feedback.
Channels: formal (follows the chain of command) and informal (the grapevine, based on social relations).
By direction: vertical (downward from superiors, upward from subordinates), horizontal or lateral (between equals) and diagonal (different levels and departments).
Importance: better job performance, willing cooperation, better decisions, makes delegation possible, aids coordination and builds morale.
Barriers in the book: too many organisational layers, language, status, physical distance, emotional and psychological barriers.

Coordination: harmonising group efforts for unity of action towards a common purpose; it is continuous and a responsibility of every manager. Objectives: reconcile goals, achieve all goals, harmonious relations, economy and efficiency.
topics.frame: Definition → process diagram → barriers under headings → measures → conclusion.
examples:
Example: the communication process and its channels
A sales manager writes an email (encoding) telling salespeople a price change (message) through the company mail (medium). Salespeople read and interpret it (decoding) and reply with questions (feedback).
Downward: the manager's instruction. Upward: a salesperson's report. Horizontal: the sales and production managers sort out a delivery date. Grapevine: a rumour about bonuses spreads over tea.
A barrier: technical jargon the new salespeople don't understand.

topics.name: Controlling
topics.summary: Meaning, nature, principles, advantages and limitations of control; control techniques.
points: Control: checking whether actions go as planned and correcting them so they conform to the plan.
Characteristics: pervasive, continuous, based on planning, action is its essence, forward-looking, delegation is key, helps cope with uncertainty.
Importance: adjusts operations, fixes managerial responsibility, has a psychological effect, aids coordination, improves efficiency and effectiveness.
Process: set standards → measure performance → compare with standards and find causes of deviation → correct deviations.

Requisites of effective control include clear objectives, suitability, flexibility, self-control, strategic-point control, timely and forward-looking action, attention to the human factor and economy.
Types: physical and financial; over actual and anticipated performance; by area of operation.
Techniques — traditional: budgetary control, standard costing. Modern: break-even analysis, PERT, CPM, statistical quality control, management audit.
topics.frame: Definition → process chart → principles → merits and limits → conclusion.
examples:
Example: control in a biscuit factory
Standard: 10,000 packets per shift with at most 1% rejects.
Measure: today's shift made 9,200 packets with 3% rejects.
Compare and find causes: a worn-out oven belt caused the stoppage and uneven baking.
Correct: replace the belt and schedule preventive maintenance (a forward-looking step so it does not happen again).

topics.name: Financial Management & Sources of Finance
topics.summary: Functions and objectives of financial management, wealth maximisation, venture capital, lease, shares.
points: Financial management: planning, organising, directing and controlling the raising and use of a firm's funds.
Functions in the book: estimate capital needs, decide capital composition, choose sources of funds, invest funds, dispose of surplus, manage cash and exercise financial control.
Objectives: regular and adequate funds, best use of funds, fair return. The debate is profit maximisation vs wealth maximisation; shareholder wealth maximisation is treated as the main goal.

Sources of funds: equity shares (ownership, permanent capital), debentures (long-term borrowing at a fixed rate), venture capital (investment in start-ups with long-term growth potential) and lease financing (use of an asset without owning it — like a hire agreement).
Primary market: new securities issued for the first time (e.g. IPO), raising funds for companies. Secondary market: existing securities are traded.
SEBI regulates the securities market to protect investors, develop the market and regulate it.
topics.frame: Definition → functions or objectives as headed points → conclusion.
examples:
Example: choosing sources of finance
A company needs ₹10 crore for a new plant. It raises ₹6 crore through equity shares (permanent capital, no fixed charge) and ₹4 crore through debentures at 9% (fixed interest, but cheaper and no loss of control). Its delivery trucks are taken on lease instead of being bought.
The new shares are sold through an IPO in the primary market; afterwards investors trade them on the stock exchange — the secondary market, regulated by SEBI.

topics.name: Human Resource Management
topics.summary: Functions of HRM, challenges for HR managers, HR planning, employer–employee relations, team building.
points: HRM: all activities for acquiring, using, maintaining and developing an organisation's human resources.

Functions: managerial (planning, organising, directing, controlling), operative (procurement, development, compensation, integration, maintenance, separation) and advisory (to top management and department heads).
Human resource planning: forecasting the organisation's future need for people and planning how to meet it; job analysis finds the tasks and skills a job requires.
Skills of HR professionals include interpersonal, communication, negotiation, problem-solving and conflict management, ethical, strategic and technology skills.
Challenges: responding to market change, managing HR globally, CSR and sustainability, using technology, controlling costs while keeping talent, demographic and diversity changes.
Employee empowerment gives staff at all levels authority to decide on their own; employee engagement is being psychologically involved in and committed to the job.
Team: two or more people interacting to reach a common goal; can be formal (command team, committee, quality circle) or informal.
Stages of team development: forming → storming → norming → performing → adjourning. Team effectiveness means meeting the team's objectives and its ability to survive.
topics.frame: Definition → functions as headed points → conclusion.
examples:
Example: HR in a new hospital wing
HR planning: the wing needs 40 nurses in six months; 10 can be moved from other wards, so 30 must be hired. Job analysis lists the tasks and skills each nursing post needs.
Operative functions follow: recruit and select (procurement), train (development), fix pay (compensation), look after welfare and safety (maintenance).
The new team goes through forming and storming (role clashes) before norming and performing.

topics.name: Choosing a Form of Organisation
topics.summary: Overview of forms and the features of an ideal form of business organisation.
points: Features of an ideal form: easy formation, limited liability, enough capital, secrecy, flexibility, stability, little government control, low tax burden, efficient management and owner interest.

No form has all the ideal features. Sole proprietorship and partnership score on easy formation, less control, owner interest, secrecy and flexibility; company and cooperative score on limited liability, capital, managerial efficiency and stability.
Factors in choosing a form: nature of business, volume of business, area of operation, capital needed, control desired, expected life of the business and level of regulation accepted.

Book's conclusion: sole proprietorship for small business, partnership for somewhat larger business, private company for medium business, public company for large business, cooperative to protect a particular group's interest.
At expansion the owner can keep the existing form or move to a new one.
topics.frame: List forms → table comparing them on the features above → conclude with a reasoned choice.
examples:
Example: matching the form to the business
A tea stall → sole proprietorship (small, easy to start). Three friends starting a CA firm → partnership (skills pooled, moderate capital). A family firm making auto parts for car makers → private company (medium size, limited liability). A steel plant needing ₹500 crore from thousands of investors → public company. Weavers who want to escape middlemen → cooperative society.

topics.name: Multinational Corporations
topics.summary: Why firms become multinational; issues, trends and controversies of MNCs.
points: International business: trade in goods, services and aids to trade between two or more countries.
Importance: spreads technology, drives globalisation, better use of resources, faster growth, more goods and jobs, lower costs and more government revenue.
MNC: a company with subsidiaries and affiliates in many countries, under central control, aiming at global profit maximisation.
Why firms become multinational: economies of scale, a growing world market, response to foreign competition, lower costs, avoiding tariffs and using technological strength.
Features: large size, large foreign sales, many products, command over technology and innovation, a common pool of resources and a common strategy for affiliates.

Issues and controversies: conflict with host-country interests, high profit orientation, reluctance to transfer technology, restrictive practices, transfer pricing, few top posts for locals, balance-of-payments strain, weak local linkages, influence over host governments.
topics.frame: Definition → reasons → merits and demerits → conclusion.
examples:
Example: how an MNC works and where it clashes
A car maker headquartered abroad sets up a subsidiary in India, sells cars here and exports parts to its other plants — decisions on models and technology come from head office (central control).
Benefits to India: jobs, technology, tax revenue and exports. Issues: it may buy parts from its own foreign units at high prices (transfer pricing) to show lower profit in India, and keep top posts and key technology at home.
